title: GAL, MICHALLE. Aestheticism: Deep Formalism and the Emergence of Modernist Aesthetics. Bern, Switzerland: Peter Lang AG International Academic Publishers, 2015, 166 pp., 6 color illus., $60.95 paper.
abstract: Has the development of analytic aesthetics in the twentieth century led us astray? Michalle Gal suggests it has in her new book Aestheticism. Gal's thesis and theory are simultaneously radical and familiar. She seeks to reconstruct and reassert a modernist aesthetic theory (which includes a theory of the essence of art) from the late nineteenth century and early twentieth century with some alterations and amendments. In doing so, she rehearses the history of two related moments in art, art theorizing, and criticism: aestheticism and formalism. She demonstrates that these two theories are fecund for the construction of a new theory. Gal judiciously uses quotations from primary sources (Whistler, Pater, Wilde, Fry, Bell), and very helpful color plates (six) of paintings by Whistler, Albert Moore, Henry Landseer, and Jasper Johns. Gal attempts to rescue aestheticism and early formalism from the typical criticism that these theories are too extreme (or superficial) with respect to their concentration on formal and surface qualities. From the beginning of the book, Gal sets up a foil to her new theory: what she calls “linguistic aesthetics or symbolic aesthetics.” By this she means the influence of the philosophy of language (inter alia) on twentieth century, analytic (or Anglo‐American) aesthetics. Gal begins by discussing the famous Whistler versus Ruskin trial of 1878. She finds the issues broached in this trial instructive. Ruskin represents the pre‐modernist, mimetic view of art, while Whistler is coming to terms with what will eventually develop into aestheticism and early formalism. Chapter 1 broaches the merger of content and form and the practical anti‐realism of aestheticism‐formalism. Practical anti‐realism involves the recognition of art as a “detached and autonomous ontological sphere” (p. 18), and thereby liberation from the mimetic, realist representation of nature and the world. Aestheticists prescribe that artists must develop “cultivated blindness”: non‐naturalism as artificiality, i.e., they must create an autonomous, internal order in art, not an imitation of natural order. In addition, Gal discusses “untranslatability” of external meanings or ideas from one medium to another, which implies the uniqueness of each artistic medium, and thereby the dichotomy of form and content dissolves. Chapter 2 begins with an interesting discussion of the distinction between visual and conceptual mimesis. Visual mimesis is the pre‐modern, traditional definition of mimesis. Conceptual mimesis, which is a product of linguistic aesthetics, is committed to the idea that form and content are separable. The artwork becomes (centrally) an intellectual object, not a sensual one. The artwork becomes complete when interpreted by the viewer or critic. In addition, this conceptual mimesis permits the inversion of what aestheticism considers internal and external properties of an artwork. According to Gal, linguistic aesthetic theory claims that an artwork is a “symbol whose core essence lies in its content” (p. 13). She claims that once one determines content as the essence, this leads to “translation” problems. Contents may be expressed in different media—e.g., sound (music), text (literature), color and shape (painting)—or from one artwork to another. For example, if a poem can be paraphrased (“translated”), what is paraphrased or summarized is its content. Aestheticist‐formalists disagree that this can be achieved; it requires a misunderstanding of the nature of an artwork. Putting aside other issues in aesthetic epistemology and testimony, one might as well read the CliffsNotes. Also in Chapter 2, Gal introduces two important concepts for her aestheticism‐formalism: “introversiveness” and “un‐recruitability.” (Some of the terminology Gal uses and coins is cumbersome.) Introversive art absorbs external properties or referents into the form. “Cultural charge” is already “materially dwelling in the form” (p. 64). I take “cultural charge” to be an amalgam of symbolic meanings, codes, thematic meanings, and associations that people discern or infer from certain formal properties and materials. Introversion is also important in establishing artistic freedom, which is derived (perhaps paradoxically) from the artist's self‐restraint in adhering to the limits and requirements of the medium being used. This is in juxtaposition to the notion of artistic freedom in linguistic aesthetic theory, which locates freedom in expansionism—stretching the limits of the various media (e.g., theatrical works without narrative, music without sound). It may be similar to claiming that excessive freedom is no freedom at all; freedom must exist within a framework of constraints. “Un‐recruitability” refers to art being “structurally immune to external conquest” (p. 100). For example, artificial beauty is not supposed to remind the spectator of natural beauty. Content is fused to form, and they cannot be separated. These concepts, along with untranslatability, sound like a strong form of medium‐specificity. Mysteriously, the now common term “medium‐specificity” is not used. Introversiveness and un‐recruitability account for the autonomy of art. Furthermore, prescriptively, an artist has obligations to the requirements and limitations of the medium in which she works, but she has no external obligations (this is part of the meaning of the dictum “art for art's sake” associated with aestheticism). Chapter 3 addresses the concept of syntacticity and musicality. Syntacticity is the internal arrangement of material within an artwork. Here, there is disagreement among the aestheticians themselves. Wilde argues that the literary arts are the highest among art forms; Pater argues that music is the highest; and Whistler argues that painting is the highest. Probably this debate is pointless, but the point of attempting such hierarchies here is worthwhile. Because of the aestheticist‐formalist goal to privilege the internal order and arrangement of materials in art, music becomes the best example of how this can be achieved. Music then functions as an analogy to how the other art forms can achieve a kind of “musicality.” Chapter 4 discusses the way in which aestheticism‐formalism divorces art from life—it seeks a detachment of one from the other that helps to emphasize artificiality in art. In one important section, Gal attempts to explicate her concept of “deep form”—a central concept in the book. Pinning it down is difficult. From what I can gather, deep form consists in the artwork's formal properties imbued with some combination of aesthetic and artistic properties. In the last chapter, Gal says: “Accordingly, deep form is such that it absorbs material and non‐material elements as content, meaning, idea, and thought. The form renders non‐material elements unextractable from it and subordinated to its internal arrangement. Thus they, in turn, render the form deep” (p. 152). In chapter 5, Gal explains the concept of the “completeness” of the artwork in aestheticism. Completeness of an artwork consists in internal order, ontological independence, and a particular conception of beauty. Chapter 6 addresses the nature and role of criticism. Gal claims that criticism plays two roles in aestheticism. First, criticism enforces the limits of media. Second, criticism gives rise to new artworks. On this view, criticism does not interpret artworks, but encourages new ones. The reception of art consists in absorption and a focus on experience, not the extraction of cognitive value. Art is primarily spirit edification. Gal's combination of altered elements from aestheticism and early formalism is called deep formalism, which is intended to be a complete theory of art. This includes a definition of the artwork as deep form. Thus, the essential features of an artwork are opacity, un‐recruitability, introversiveness, non‐reflective yet productive symbolism, freedom, and completeness. Other terms may serve Gal's theoretical goals more effectively and would reduce the inelegance of some of these neologisms. Currently, there are terms that could have been employed with suitable modifications (e.g., medium‐specificity, autonomism). Often it is difficult to determine the boundaries of these concepts, if there are boundaries. If there are no strict differences in meaning, then the surfeit of concepts is puzzling. At the end of chapter 3, Gal offers an interpretation of Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest. The play is meant to serve as an exemplar for the aestheticist‐formalist artwork par excellence and to demonstrate the workings of the theory. To claim that the play is about Victorian manners and mores (“referential manifesto against the hypocrisy of Victorian social conduct” [p. 84]) already misunderstands the artwork. The problem inheres in the idea that “the play is about …” What follows “about” is some meaning (or referring to) that is external to the “world” of the play itself. According to Gal and her aestheticist‐formalist allies, interpreting artworks in this way has a cost: the ignoring or devaluing of the formal features of the artwork, its artificiality, and perhaps, most importantly, such a reading causes misunderstanding of the artwork's essential features. One wonders precisely why the two critical practices are opposed, or why one denigrates the other. Focusing on both the formal properties of the play and its thematic meaning are useful in interpreting the play; both methods can produce true statements about the play, and, for the most part, one can be put forward without negating the other. But is it plausible to believe that Wilde intended the play to be about language only? Gal argues that Wilde did, and cites some of Wilde's own criticism that substantiates this claim. Some critics might reply that the critique of language is (or is analogous to) the critique of codes. In other words, the play addresses both language and Victorian social conduct. One might even be tempted to say that the one serves the other. But therein lies the rub. When there is such a division in possible interpretations, there is an inclination to say that the aestheticist‐formalist one serves the thematic one (external content). Once again, form is subordinated to content. Thus, Gal supports the idea that the play meets all of the aestheticist‐formalist criteria and therefore has no separable content. If the last line of the play (“I've now realized for the first time in my life the vital Importance of Being Earnest”) is referring to the word “earnest” (both as an adjective and twice as a proper noun [title of the play, name], which is achieved through homonymic ambiguity by its being uttered in performance), then one cannot claim without contradiction that “Earnest” refers to the rigid designator of the name “Earnest.” Gal makes the case that even the characters of Gwendolyn and Cecily possess anti‐realist theories of language. They want to marry men named “Earnest.” They care about the name only. When one posits that one artistic goal serves another, namely, that form serves content, then one is privileging the one function of art that also makes art's existence problematic. This is exactly the situation that aestheticism‐formalism criticizes and rejects. Gal begins the last chapter with a question: “Why did modernism in aesthetics collapse?” (p. 145). Did it collapse, or did it transform or evolve? Furthermore, there is a difference between modernist art evolving, or at least giving rise to, new kinds of art, new genres, etc., and modernist aesthetic theory being discredited, refuted, or at least developed into a presumably more cogent aesthetic theory. Since the first‐order art changed, the theory had to change with it. Besides, this diagnosis seems to suppose that there is a unified, consensus theory of art in the rarefied world of aesthetics. Obviously, that is not the case. Another potential shortcoming is that Gal relies exclusively on two philosophers for her exposition of linguistic aesthetics or symbolic aesthetics: Nelson Goodman and Arthur Danto. Obviously and justifiably, Goodman and Danto are pillars of contemporary aesthetics. Nonetheless, I think most aestheticians would find using Goodman's and Danto's work as emblematic of analytic aesthetics as too narrow and certainly insufficient for making generalizations about analytic aesthetics and/or this historical period of aesthetics. To be fair, analytic aesthetics is not necessarily equivalent to what Gal calls linguistic aesthetics—linguistic aesthetics may be one sub‐part or version of analytic aesthetics. Certainly analytic aesthetics developed from the significant foundations Goodman and Danto provided, but there are many other sources—and many significantly different from Goodman and Danto (one thinks of Wollheim). While there is no doubt that the philosophy of language has influenced every branch of philosophy in the twentieth century, this influence, especially in aesthetics, has not resulted in a universal or unified treatment or application of the linguistic concepts and tools. For example, Gal objects to the notion of symbol in linguistic aesthetics, external/internal distinction, and reliance upon an artwork's relationship to external referents, concerns, and values. Gal is suggesting that the tenets of aestheticism and early formalism better reflect what artists do or should do (more on that in a moment). In linguistic aesthetics, the concept of symbol involves “reflective referentiality” and transparency. In other words, the artwork, or a part thereof, is more or less transparently referring to some object or event in the world—the world external to the artwork itself. Gal prefers substituting “productive referentiality,” which produces new referents, not preexisting or preconceived referents. A productive referent is a “result of its own ‘material’ or compositional qualities” (p. 13). This is (perhaps) a cogent criticism of the linguistic aesthetics of Goodman and Danto, but it does not apply to many other theories in this tradition. Simply consider the work of Dickie, Carroll, Levinson, Kivy, and Stephen Davies from the past forty years. One detects a straw man argument. One important value of this book is Gal's demonstration of interesting and cogent comparisons between the aestheticists and the early formalists. However, many questions remain. Is there confusion about whether a theory of art should be descriptive or prescriptive or both? If prescriptive, then how can the aestheticist‐formalist insist on the freedom and autonomy that is central to these theories? It seems that the aestheticist‐formalist seeks to influence artistic practices, whereas the descriptivist approach is explanatory. To wit, given the history of artistic practices and the kinds of thing people have called art, the goal of descriptivist theories of art is to establish or acquire the essential features of art and artworks. Which is Gal pursuing? Is there an implicit acceptance of the honorific sense of “art” and a rejection of a classificatory sense? There is no outright condemnation of contemporary art, but if, for example, conceptual art cannot be subsumed under deep formalism, then one is confronted with a false dilemma. One either rejects conceptual art as art, or one is forced to pay attention to features of conceptual art that probably miss the point. The goal is to discover a way for the content to be, to a certain extent, separable from, or external to, the artwork while avoiding the substitutivity problem or dissolving it. Indeed, this is a difficult problem. Contemporary discussions of, say, which properties are part of the identity conditions of an artwork are descriptive projects. Now, there are prescriptive or normative concerns, but those have to do with what one might call meta‐ontological issues. Analytic aestheticians recognize the role that evaluation may play in developing metaphysical theories: what we value in artworks, as evidenced by critical practices, helps to determine which properties are essential to an artwork. But this valuing comes ex post facto, after the artwork has been produced; it is not meant to determine artistic practices. One learns a considerable amount of valuable information about Whistler, Pater, Wilde, Fry, and Bell. Elements of Gal's theory should be taken seriously as a bellwether. Alternative theories to the often‐unwarranted focus on reductive notions of artwork content need to be developed. And for those interested in the modern period of art and criticism, this book should be read.

title: Alex Baine'sWomen's Emancipation in Uganda
abstract: all photos by author except where otherwise notedAlex Baine is a contemporary Ugandan woman artist who graduated from the Margaret Trowell School of Industrial and Fine Art (or MTSIFA) in 1989.1 During her final year, she painted a large work, Women's Emancipation in Uganda (Fig. 1) (1989), in which she represented women in domestic and nondomestic (conventional and unconventional) economies, spaces, and histories. Baine has not produced any other painting since her graduation.2 It is evident that Baine's art career, like those of several other female graduates of the Art School, has been interrupted by many issues including family, business, further education, and diversion into other professions.3 However, in this article I acknowledge that she championed women's emancipation in Uganda's contemporary art in the 1980s, a debate that I trace in her work.Baine painted Women's Emancipation in Uganda under the instruction of Francis Musangogwantamu (1923–2007), who himself was a student of Margaret Trowell from 1954 to 1958. Baine explains that:Her explanation is revealing. First, Uganda has a rich tradition of craft-making. However contemporary art is not directly related to this tradition. Instead it is a product of formal education. This is why most of Baine's work was done under the supervision of Musangogwantamu—a leading artist and art educator. Secondly, it follows logically from the artist's statement that, although done under supervision, the work was based on personal choice and an individual reading and interpretation of history—it is an individual's artistic expression. Thirdly, Baine allows us to understand the fact that, beyond the satisfaction of academic requirements, the artist used her work to archive changes in the plight of women in Uganda—a record which is important to this article as well as to contemporary art in Uganda.Baine leads the viewer into the painting through a mundane domestic economy in which women perform chores such as mat-making, basketry, food preparation, and child-nurturing. She based her choice of subjects and activities on certain traditional conventions which gender domestic chores and responsibilities. Three women sit in the foreground. To the left, two are involved in mat-weaving and basketry. To the right, a woman is cooking food in front of another woman, who raises a pestle to pound dry ration in a mortar with a baby strapped on her back. Unlike the women in the foreground, who are wearing busuuti, she is wearing a ssuuka.5 She, like the other three, is thus identified as “traditional,” using traditional dress codes. A little girl sits next to the mortar. Without interrupting, she observes, and learns, the different activities that the older women perform. Another older woman walks past her, balancing a pot on her head and carrying a baby in her left hand.Critics view these as perfunctory chores grounded in the belief that women's contribution to the rural/domestic economy has no monetary value. The patriarchal society in Uganda perceives and applauds women who do domestic chores as wives and mothers who produce food and care for their households, nothing more (Bantebya and McIntosh 2006:1). Society takes them for granted. The mentoring cited here, which assumes that girls inherit their mothers’ trades, is a process of socialization that marks, maps, and appropriates gender roles while marginalizing women in Uganda (Matembe 2002:4). Socialization then becomes a powerful device used to counter women's claim for equality and self-actualization. Thus Baine, like the wider society, alludes to the widely held view that traditions are passed on from old to young, mother to child. She gives visual expression to child-mentoring, an important form of informal education and transfer of indigenous knowledge which has kept many traditions in Uganda alive. Many women do these things in the countryside. During periods of low agricultural activity, women make crafts as recreation and also to produce household items. Baine is aware of this reality and the way it confines a woman to the domestic economy where a woman's role is, saying:Such confinement is often legitimated, socialized, and propagated across generations. It highlights the assumption that women are valued for their contributions within the family and perceived and applauded as wives and mothers who produce food and care for their households (Bantebya and McIntosh 2006:1). In the process, women are taken for granted and viewed as “passive sexual objects, as devoted mothers, and dutiful wives” (Rosaldo and Lamphere 1974:1).However it is also known that historically some women in Uganda have refused to be marginalized. For example, in 1892 Sir Henry Edward Colville, a military and a commissioner of Uganda, signed a protectorate agreement. The document outlawed slavery. It also set in motion a process of negotiations that culminated in the signing of the 1900 Buganda Agreement—a comprehensive document which fixed the borders of the Buganda Kingdom and laid the foundations of Uganda's modern statehood, which was confirmed through the 1902 Order in Council. Some women took advantage of these colonial laws on freedom and liberty that came along with the policies. Waliggo (2002:29) writes, for example, that “soon, both Catholic and Protestant missionaries regretted the effects of freedom on women, when women of the household of Kaggo, a county chief … refused to cook.” As a result, the missionaries turned around and accused women of misusing freedom and of being lazy. Waliggo cites a missionary named Walker, who argued that:In other words, the new freedoms engendered inherent contradictions and invited a new set of gendered negotiations and colonial ordinances to police women. Clearly Musisi (1991) traces the early gendered struggles against nonconforming women in Uganda and the issues which informed such struggles. She shows how the early attempts to control women's rights forced a coalition of the State, the Church, and traditional institutions—a coalition which became even harsher in the 1970s when Field Marshal Idi Amin Dada enacted decrees to remove women from the public space.Intriguingly, Baine is aware of this history. She therefore did not seek to propagate this domestic economy in her artwork. For example, her representation of child nurturing is not conventional. The women she portrays carry one child each, and as such, the artist's notion of motherhood appears to contradict Uganda's conventional wisdom, which defines the fertility of a woman in terms of the number of children she produces. Explaining her symbolism and its sources, Baine narrates that, during her education at secondary school, she participated in a “Family Planning Competition” and won a prize:This recollection helps us to see how her participation in discussions on women's reproductive rights sharpened and shaped Women's Emancipation in Uganda. Tripp contends that discussions on women's “reproductive rights” (2002:4), which started in the late 1980s, became very relevant to women's lives. Through them, Tripp adds, women's groups emerged in order to lobby against female circumcision, domestic violence, and rape, while promoting sex education and family planning. In the work discussed here, Baine archived this women's lobby, its intentions and its successes. Baine's representation of one child per mother thus becomes emancipative. Furthermore, the craft-making portrayed in Baine's work is an economic activity through which women have improved their lives (Snyder 2000).In Women's Emancipation in Uganda, behind the women engaging in a domestic economy there is portrayal of a woman clad in military fatigues carrying a baby and holding a rifle in her right hand. In 1981, women joined a rebellion through which the National Resistance Movement took power in 1986. This participation in a political struggle was a path to self-discovery, better rights, and power (Byanyima and Mugisha 2003:118) and, for Gertrude Njuba, a decorated female officer in the Uganda Peoples’ Defence Forces, “revenge” against Obote's injustices.6 This is the radical story Baine locates in the center of her painting, using a powerful woman clad in military uniform. She carries a baby and frees the other hand to hold an assault rifle—a Kalashnikov. A gun in Uganda is a weapon whose possession gives one immense power. Many presidents have relied on their monopoly over the gun to claim and assert their power, which has affected women in specific ways. For example, during the 1981–1986 rebellion, government soldiers opened the wombs of pregnant women and indiscriminately raped in a manner that artist Muwonge Kyazze depicts in his painting Misfortune (1985) (Fig. 2).Baine's representation is therefore a giant step in the visual representation Uganda's sociopolitical negotiations using the mother and child symbolism. She—unlike Kyazze, and Maloba in his Independence monument (Fig. 3)—makes women possessors of the instruments of coercion, power, and authority. The child in this case has become subordinate. Baine's woman is active in national politics and not passive like the one in Semulya's Nation Building (1987) (Fig. 4), where children and mothers dominate a starving postwar public being served with relief supplies by energetic, industrious men. Baine does not want to take women's agency away from them.Baine's work draws heavily from the 1981–1986 rebellion during which several women combatants actively participated in gathering intelligence and at the frontlines. This account is often underestimated. For example, Kenneth Kakuru is a Judge in Uganda's Court of Appeals. At a recent symposium7 at the Uganda Museum, he argued that men make wars and go to wars to protect women. Gertrude Njuba would object to Kakuru's argument. During our interview in 2006, she told me that she went to war to protect her husband, who was being hunted by the soldiers of the Uganda Army8 because he was a member of National Resistance Movement, supported the rebellion. She left her children with her sister to join the National Resistance Army (NRA) in 1981. Joy Mirembe was the “lady who braved the dangerous route of taking the [NRA] fighters to the bush” (Kutesa 2006:168). She died in the war zone while giving birth. Dora Kuteesa was another female fighter, married to Pecos Kuteesa, who narrated in his autobiography that Dora gave birth to a daughter, nicknamed “Sergeant,” who almost lost her life in the middle of heavy gunfire (Kutesa 2006:160). As such, in Women's Emancipation in Uganda Baine records and acknowledges the role of mothers in Uganda's radical political history—a role which is often downplayed.Behind the female soldier in Women's Emancipation in Uganda, the artist presents a medical facility with a patient lying in bed. A woman is portrayed wearing a white coat with a stethoscope around her neck, which indicates that she is a doctor. She takes notes in a book in front of a patient assisted by a male nurse. Baine's hospital scene recalls the painting Harvesting Cotton (1988) (Fig. 5), by Francis Ifee, who was one of her lecturers. Ifee presents a mother and a sick child seated on a bed. The mother who is wearing a busuuti, looks down on the sick, naked child. Ifee uses dress, and dress codes, to identify his doctor as male, elite, and professional. To distinguish him from the vulnerable mother and her sick child, Ifee drapes the mother with a busuuti while he leaves the child naked. By using a female doctor treating a male patient, Baine subverts the stereotype of women as patients who rely on the help of men and instead represents men as patients, making men vulnerable.Arguably, Baine introduces women into the medical profession where they were few by the late 1980s. Although the graduation of the first woman medical doctor in Uganda took place in the 1940s, the medical profession has more female nurses and midwives than doctors. This is because these low-level categories of medical practice have been preserved for women since the colonial days of Sir Albert Cook.In 1897, Albert Cook and Katherine Thompson (later Mrs. Cook) arrived in Uganda as Church Missionary Society (CMS) missionaries to establish a medical structure.9Bantebya and McIntosh (2006:61) observe that “midwifery was the first medically related career to open to African women” following the 1915 smallpox epidemic.
