title: Arthur Miller's Century: Essays Celebrating the 100th Birthday of America's Great Playwright
abstract: As Stephen Marino rightly observes in his introduction to Arthur Miller's Century: Essays Celebrating the 100th Birthday of America's Great Playwright, this rich anthology of essays explores Miller's work from a wide range of approaches—“biographical, historical, political, comparative, language, psychology, feminist, cognitive, and dramatic theory and stagecraft” (xvii). The collection offers broad perceptions spanning the scope of Miller's texts and interesting insights into works not often treated. The brief abstracts following confirm the accuracy of Marino's assessment. Virtually all the contributions bear witness to Enoch Brater's claim in the foreword that “[e]ven after more than half a century [Miller's] voice rings true with alarming clarity” (xi).The anthology begins with two well-argued pieces, one extending across Miller's entire canon and the other focused on two earlier texts. The first chapter is a reprint of Christopher Bigsby's keynote address at the Arthur Miller Centennial Conference in 2015, titled “Performance and Arthur Miller.” The most eminent of Miller scholars, Bigsby applies his thesis to the whole of Miller's career and perceptively examines the sometimes ironic and ambivalent nature of “performance” that underlies the social and political realm and the private self. He argues that although “Miller's theatre was not polemical except at the very beginning when … he wrote plays for the trade union movement … he did write plays that staged the private consequences of private actions” (16), performance being an elemental human trait both onstage and off.Whereas Bigsby's contribution covers the whole sweep of Miller's work, Brenda Murphy's following essay centers on his seldom-discussed early attempt to write war journalism, Situation Normal. She explains Miller's growing anxiety when he unsuccessfully worked on a screenplay for producer Lester Cowan based on Ernie Pyle's Here Is Your War and discovered that the soldiers he tried to understand possessed a “personal faith in love for each other” that was “a far more potent factor … than any abstract belief” (22). Murphy explains Miller's epiphany as it is later reflected in All My Sons. As she concludes, the play “is in some sense the artistic outgrowth of the internal conflict that Miller records in Situation Normal … a play in which human relations have trumped ideological belief” (26).After these two persuasive studies, sixteen varied essays complete this major contribution to understanding the nature and significance of Miller's work. George Monteiro's “Gold, Football, and Arthur Miller's Death of a Salesman” contends that a primary source for the play was the story of a legendary football coach at the University of Michigan, Gustave “Dutch” Ferbert, who after two highly successful years abandoned the university to join in the Alaskan gold rush, vowing to return only after making it rich. Ten years later, he did just that and came back with a million dollars in hand. Monteiro claims “that ‘Dutch’ and his story was the inspiration behind Miller's creation of Ben” (31) and that his tale was a shaping resource for much of the play.Citing reader-response theory's challenge to the idea of “a universal response to a given play or work,” Ramon Espejo Romero proposes reading “the unexplored global dramas of Arthur Miller's work” (37). His essay, “From ‘Universal’ to ‘Global’ Miller: Re-Writing the History of American Drama (Historian at Work),” recounts the history of drama in Spain leading to the repressive period of Francoism when Death of a Salesman was ironically the first major American play staged after the Madrid agreements in 1953. The Franco regime allowed the performance to deny that “Francoism was in fear of foreign culture” (42); however, despite the effort to interpret the play on the regime's terms, it transformed Spanish theater even though the play is so seemingly different from the Catholic culture of the country. Romero contends that it was “a Trojan horse” that shattered Francoist culture (40). He shows how Salesman, as well as The Crucible and After the Fall, introduced a “global perspective” that expanded “the limits of theater and literary studies” generally and “the Spanish theatre aesthetic” in particular (49).Brian Mazeski's contribution, “The Salesman at Sea: Aquatic Imagery in Death of a Salesman,” reflects the growing analysis of Miller criticism in response to the often expressed complaints of the dramatist's supposedly unsophisticated and unpoetic use of language. Building on earlier defenders of Miller's language, including Matthew Roudané, Stephen Marino, and Will Smith, he convincingly analyzes the aquatic imagery in the play to illustrate “Miller's unique dramatic idiom” (87).Matt Lorenz's “‘The Lightning of My Being’: The Byronic Struggle and Apotheosis of John Proctor” discusses how Proctor in The Crucible possesses many traits of the Byronic hero. Because of Byron's identity as essentially a poet of verse romances and poems, he may “seem to have more in common with the aspirations of novelists than of dramatists” and so “seems an unlikely influence on a twentieth-century American like Miller” (71). In fact, Lorenz contends, the Byronic hero parallels much “of the flawed nature of Miller's complicated heroes” (71).Richard Brucher's “Pragmatism and the Common Man” (a play on Miller's “Tragedy and the Common Man”) explores how the Arthur Miller associated with American Stalinists in the forties evolved by the early fifties into “a notorious anti-anti-Communist, a type of knee-jerk liberal” directly opposed by the recognized philosopher of pragmatism Sidney Hook and his followers. To Brucher, however, Miller's plays, and especially A View From the Bridge, reveal how pragmatism underlies the tragic dimension of his work. Centering on View, he characterizes Eddie Carbone's “pragmatic choices” and “defiance of agonizing, pragmatic choices” (80). In sum, Miller's dramas “help us know … how to anticipate unexpected consequences of our acts, especially if we believe that practical actions are necessary tests of our thoughts” (82). Garin Cycholl also addresses A View From the Bridge in “That World Fallen to Stones,” noting the similarities between Saul Bellow's Augie March and Eddie Carbone as characters caught between two worlds, a mythical old order and the new one “where everything has a price tag” (87). Comparing and contrasting the one- and two-act versions of the text, Cycholl describes Eddie's conflicted loyalties to the mythic old world represented by “the docks” and the need to cross over the boundaries into an emerging order. In his view, the docks appear “as a village” and provide the setting “for a distinctly ‘American’ tragedy” (89).In what will prove a controversial piece, Stefani Koorey exposes Arthur Miller's blatant sexism in “Arthur Miller Unzipped.” Beginning with how Miller exploited his relationship with Marilyn Monroe to direct attention away from his appearance before the House Un-American Activities Committee, she traces how he also exploited female characters in his plays—“Miller fabricates his female characters to serve the dramas of his decidedly masculine protagonists…. Women in Miller's literature are primarily configured to substitute or divert attention from the male action” (95). Koorey's unqualified condemnation of Miller's “patriarchal literary world view” (96) presents a formidable challenge to those who wish to question her claim. Some critics have, of course, contested parts of her argument in reference to given works and female characters, but the breadth of the case against Miller's treatment of women both on the stage and off will likely provoke other lively debate. Not exactly “celebrating … America's great playwright,” her essay is the most controversial text in this highly provocative anthology.Sylvia Kasey Marks interestingly directs attention to Miller's stories that critics have pretty much ignored or analyzed for essentially autobiographical references. She finds echoes from Miller's dramas in the stories, especially those collected in I Don't Need You Any More, published in 1967. She primarily assesses three tales, “I Don't Need You Any More,” “Fitter's Night,” and Jane's Blanket, describing how they all mirror the plays and potentially provide “a gloss on all of Miller's work” (117). In another convincing comparative study, Paul J. Contino presents a probing analysis of the idea of nadryv in The Brothers Karamazov and The Price, “Nadryv in New York: Dostoevskian Lacerations in Arthur Miller's The Price.” Noting Miller's long admiration of The Brothers Karamazov (he first read it as a teenager and at one point plotted writing it as a screenplay that might conceivably allow Marilyn Monroe to play Grushenka), Contino highlights the striking similarities between Victor and Walter Franz and Zosima and Alyosha. Both works portray nadryv, he asserts, “the lacerating psycho-spiritual dynamic in which characters perversely enact by playing a false role of self-sacrifice, in order to gain power in the eyes of another” (120). The next essay addresses another seldom-examined text, The Creation of the World and Other Business. Frank Bergmann looks at “Archetype and the Rhythm of Decorum” in the infrequently staged play and draws the intriguing conclusion that Northrop Frye may well have been right in asserting that though the play is hardly Miller's “best goddamned play,” as the playwright once declared, “it may well be his most central” (133).Ann Hall's “‘The Times, They Are A-Changin’: Time and Politics in Arthur Miller's Broken Glass and Harold Pinter's Ashes to Ashes” is the last extensive comparative study in the collection. Hall argues with insightful readings that in confronting the Holocaust both dramatists employ time in a “non-realistic” way that dissolves the seeming distinction often drawn between Miller's so-called realistic vision and Pinter's association with the absurdists. Both employ “methods that not only dissolve the years between the historical event and the present, but also dissolve the traditional distinctions used to describe their works” (135). Her engaging readings of both texts invite others to contest the often simplistic attempts to label Miller's work. Both dramas, Hall asserts, depict the Holocaust “from an altruistic spatial and temporal vantage point” and “connect political and domestic violence” (141)—and both portray the leading female characters as agents of necessary change “in terms of past, present, and future” (143).The remaining contributors to the anthology are especially well-known Miller scholars. In “The Last Yankee: Tragedy and Two Kinds of Pride,” David Palmer, the current president of the Arthur Miller Society, answers why Miller called The Last Yankee “a comedy about a tragedy.” Palmer sees the text “as a portal toward understanding Miller's broader vision of tragedy,” especially “a peculiarly American tragedy” and how it “rises from a faulty sense of pride … grounded in the dark side of the American dream” (145). In his thorough exploration of the text, he reveals how the play resonates with other Miller texts in dramatizing how the sense of pride generated by the absurd notion of the American Dream translates “from authentic pride to hubristic pride” (158). This cogently argued essay resurrects long pursued questions about Miller's concept of tragedy in a culture that seemingly challenges its very nature.In one of the most impressive studies in this collection, Jane K. Dominik, past president of the Arthur Miller Society, provides an inventive and convincing treatment of absent characters in Miller's plays beginning with They Too Arise and extending to the end of his career. “Empty Chairs, Pools of Light: Absent Characters in Arthur Miller's Drama” surveys the broad range of “characters who never appear on stage in the present time” but “become central to characters' conflicts, motivations, and dilemmas” (162). Dominik illuminates the ways Miller employs “objects, lights, music, conjuring, unseen Listeners, or silent bodies” to project absent figures and shows how these various strategies move “his play away from so-called realistic drama to impressionism, abstract expressionism, symbolism, surrealism, absurdism, minimalism, and magical realism” (180). This penetrating and important study again opens doors to further critical analyses.The founding and current editor of The Arthur Miller Journal, Stephen Marino, dares to characterize Miller as “Brooklyn's Shakespeare.” His inventive reading investigates the “startling comparisons in their biographies” (185), not least of which how both artists lived in strikingly similar worlds. He compares the writers' histories, their families, their gradual introduction to theater, their subsequent need to leave family to pursue stage careers, their common struggles to tread “the treacherous political and religious waters of their times” (189), and, most significantly, their shared pursuit of tragedy. “Just as Shakespeare's plays defined Renaissance tragedy,” Marino concludes, “Miller's essay, ‘Tragedy and the Common Man’ re-defined tragedy for the modern era” (189). In short “Arthur Miller is Brooklyn's Shakespeare for the legacy he left” (189).Susan C. W. Abbotson, long associated with the Arthur Miller Society and Miller scholarship, also adds a highly rewarding biographical perspective in “Miller and Morath in Collaboration.” Beginning with the chilling history of Inge Morath's survival of World War II and her subsequent emergence as a world-class photographer whose ability “to view a person's inner nature and capture it through her lens” (194) mirrors Miller's portrayal of stage characters, Abbotson labels their union “a true marriage of equals” (194). Incorporating several powerful copies of Morath's photography, she characterizes her art and summarizes her first meeting Miller and their nearly forty years together. Despite having separate careers, she notes, Morath and Miller shared a common vision and effectively worked together on three different books. Exploring these works, Abbotson discovers many “excellent insights into Miller's beliefs, fears, and hopes” and leads to the undeniable conclusion that Morath and Miller's relationship and collaboration have been “for too long critically ignored, and appear eminently worthy of closer inspection” (214).The last entry in the volume appropriately reasserts what Bigsby's initial entry contends and other essays confirm, that Miller holds an enduring place in American drama. In “Arthur Miller: A Career of Commitment,” Joshua Polster, also a past president of the Arthur Miller Society, assesses Miller's continuous commitment “to the arts and humanities in order to advance social awareness, engagement and progress” (215). His summing up highlights key stages in Miller's biography, demonstrating again how the playwright stayed true to his convictions in his life and work and repeatedly expressed “his willingness to engage in difficult conversations and take on societal problems that needed to be addressed” (229). He speaks for all Miller admirers when he argues that onstage and off, Miller's presence is felt, that his “dramas and political activism continue to serve and powerfully resonate” (231).As these brief abstracts testify, Arthur Miller's Century not only succeeds in celebrating Miller's life and work, but also offers new or redefined strategies for further exploration in its variety of approaches and insights. A centennial is surely the proper time to pay tribute, but it is also the right time to reassess, revise, and redirect the body of criticism addressing an author's life, work, and place. The far-ranging perspectives expressed in this collection give deserved acknowledgment to early studies, but open new avenues of assessment and understanding as well.

title: Subject Matters in Early Modern Art
abstract: Subject as Aporia in Early Modern Art edited by Alexander Nagel and Lorenzo, Pericolo, Burlington, VT and Farnham: Ashgate, 2010, 257 pp., 97 b. & w. illus., £65.00 This is a fascinating and important book, which introduces to a general public stimulating new ways of thinking about indeterminacy and the concept of the subject in early modern art, particularly painting. Derived from a conference session on ‘Subject as Aporia’ held at the Renaissance Society of America in 2007, the volume consists of nine chapters and a useful introduction that investigate a range of early modern artworks, including oil painting and architecture, in relation to indeterminacy. The book does not simply claim that there are multiple, or indeed infinite, interpretations of artworks all of potentially equal value. On the contrary, indeterminacy in this context is understood as part of the way in which specific early modern art works produce new questions about art, the role and potential of art making. The editors and authors are particularly interested in art works that have remained opaque or obtuse to standard modes of interpretation in the history of art or that seem to ‘lack’ a readily identifiable subject or subjects. Rather than trying to resolve that indeterminacy through stable identifications, they interrogate the ways in which such art stages or problematizes the very constitution of the subject of art. Indeterminacy, it is argued in the Introduction to the volume, was part of the rhetorical structure of many artworks whose subjects are not readily identifiable or resolvable for precisely that reason. Indeterminacy is therefore not a problem to be solved, but a productive state of potentiality in relation to the question of the subject. The editors are clearly deeply indebted to the work of Jacques Derrida in particular, but the arguments presented throughout the book are well marinated in Renaissance art theory. Thus the ambition of the project goes beyond identifying subjects through iconography and iconology to open considerations of the various ways in which early modern artworks sought to stage their own critical presence as art. The essays presented here interrogate issues arising from the shifts in relationships between aporia and subject. While the idea of the subject is a familiar one in art history, the editors wish to demonstrate the ways in which it was estranged during the early modern period via their use of the concept of ‘aporia’. The term derives from ancient Greek απορíα, literally ‘a never to be traversed path’ or ‘a blind alley’; a-poros is a blocked path; a way that has been but is not now open. This nicely paradoxical term itself indicates that there is no need to acknowledge the path itself when it is merely a means to an end, open and in use. Aporia thus forces a rethinking of the approach itself. Artworks that enter into this process, suggest the editors, anticipated the work of interpretation itself, setting differing modes of vision and different visual traditions into tension with each other. The editors resist what they see as the conventional and overly hasty resolution of the ‘subject’ in art history in which the subject of an artwork is assumed to be external to it. They argue that the ‘subject’ can be perceived dynamically as the result of a dialectic involving matter and form: ‘Subject is artistic matter already encrypted with the potentiality of its elaboration’, but subject is ‘also capable of being fundamentally and internally transformed in its elaboration’ (5). Thus accidents can contribute to the constitution of subjects, and the editors therefore see contradiction as a plausible component of artistic acts, and perhaps indeed as a necessary part of extraordinary artworks. The period between 1400 and 1600 is identified as critical in this exploration, because of the very significant shifts that affected the conditions of art making, produced new forms and estranged familiar modes of approach. As landscape became a crucial site or developed out of experimentation with subject and setting, the Reformation pressured the notion of figuration itself. Not only did new formats, genres, subjects, and techniques (printed images, oil painting, drawing) emerge and new private forms of collecting art develop, but some artworks of that period – important and exceptional works, argue the editors – display intriguing forms of indeterminacy that re-open the question of ‘subject’. Such artworks require explanation beyond that of ‘the play of the signifier’ and, suggest the editors, they are not best served by traditional modes of art-historical scholarship – particularly iconographical erudition or literary application – that assume that they simply require the identification of a fixed subject. Instead the editors propose that the systemic shifts in the early modern period made the emergence of aporetic artworks ‘a structural inevitability’ (3). The significance of the question of the subject in the context of Christian image making is particularly profound. Istorie allowed for more confusion on the part of the viewer than the icon. The fear of idolatry haunted the Judaeo-Christian tradition. The visual arts were inhabited by the possibility that they were already fictions and open to offering pleasure as works of art, rather than bearing referential content. In Byzantine icon theory and in Scholastic thinking, the charge of idolatry was repulsed on the grounds that persons and stories presented in paintings have external identities, that is, that images have subjects. The fear of worship of mere human fabrications rather than the creator threatened especially when images confused their subjects, or offered too much distracting information. After the Council of Trent of the mid-sixteenth century, clergymen such as Gabriele Paleotti, Federico Borromeo and Johannes Molanus insisted that the visual narrative or istoria of images must conform to Catholic truth. The image was seen to be appropriate, therefore, insofar as its subject matter was defined externally and was distinct from the mode or forms by which it was interrogated (indeed, these authors argued that the subject of an artwork could only emerge if presented correctly in terms of means of presentation). Thus subject steadily implied the notion of religious and pictorial propriety. Giovanni Andrea Gilio advised contemporary painters in his Dialogi (1564) as follows: ‘the good artificer is supposed to discern between accidents that are to be avoided and those that should be developed; between the ones that devalue the subject and those that embellish it’ (7). The editors approach the question of ‘subject’ (literally ‘what lies beneath’) in relation to aporia. Subjects in this period threatened to slip into aporia; this occurred, oddly enough, as a result of the fact that the very idea of subject was a form of protection against ambiguity. Since in art and literature subject steadily implied the notion of propriety in this period, the artist's work was in part to find new dispositions and expressions so that the subject became new and unique. Art was inclined to disturb decorum, thereby raising questions of its purposes, categories, preoccupations and approaches. The subject is composed therefore out of actual and also potential characteristics, residues of the artist's searching through intermediary solutions until reaching a final form. The artwork can thus be regarded as the subject of a dialectic in which meanings and characters coalesce, interweave and even conflict with each other during the artwork's process and in its finality. In this sense the process of artistic production enlivens the artwork from within. Such a definition of subject, of course, exceeds the semantic field of the term in the period under investigation. The editors forcefully defend this approach: ‘only a dynamic paradigm of interpretation – one in which actual and virtual characteristics of the artwork are taken into account – allows art historians to contend with early modern artefacts with due rigor, which is to say due flexibility’ (8). It is quite possible that artworks from other periods could be shown to be aporetic by slowing down interpretation and examining the procedures in their making in order to understand how contradictions and non-resolutions participated in their identity even as they render a fixed identity questionable. Aporetic works bring into play a potentiality that was generally only latent or subtended in art works of this period. Thus the artefact as subject is composed of actual and potential characteristics, which are the traces and remains of the artist's exploration of intermediary solutions until reaching a final form. This prompts one of the editors’ most arresting ideas (which is also one of the least excavated by their contributors), namely that an artwork's significations can also extend into future developments way beyond the range of the artist. The discussion here is at its richest in relation to artworks, which are predominantly secular. Greater attention to religious art would have further enriched this already exciting volume. In various ways the essays presented here show the work of art as encouraging reflection on the conditions under which subject matter is produced, to problematize the question of the subject and to expose the work of art as interrogating the inter-related problems of the subject, propriety, and image. Alexander Nagel's essay focuses on Giorgione's The Three Philosophers to do this. He argues that Giorgione moved from greater to lesser specificity in part to explore what painting can do to establish identity through processes of estrangement. He brilliantly links this with the long-standing suspicion about images that the Christian concern with likeness, origins and reference sought repeatedly to address, questions that were openly articulated only after Giorgione's time – during the so-called Catholic Reform – over the referential capacity of an image. Two responses are possible to this. One would be to indulge in the forms of teleology and periodization that currently afflict much of the practice of art history (along the lines that Giorgione is significant because he anticipates ideas that are articulated later); the other would be to recognize that art's making itself as art from within is a process that is made opaque precisely by the pressures towards periodization and the stabilization of the subject in art history. The significance of Giorgione's work thus emerges as its ability to draw attention to the arbitrary nature of and breaking down of boundaries between image categories. Nagel reads compositional imbalance in Giorgione in terms of ‘a basic tampering with traditional pictorial structure’ (33). A central episode is rendered unfamiliar by its curious marginalization. Thus at a level ‘deeper than style or technique’ (34) the ground of painting's relation to subject matter is shifted to question the basis of Christian art altogether. Suspension of matters in between established states are thereby seen as particularly pregnant. Rather than representing three identifiable figures in a Christian story, Nagel suggests that Giorgione's three philosophers are figurations of human knowledge in the face of nature and the cosmos. Painting is the place where homo quaerens can be exposed and thought about. The painting opens a space for the viewer to reflect on human knowledge and the role of images in it. The image images imaging. At its most glib the argument risks dissolving into the familiar ‘art is about art’ cliché that dominates so much discussion of modern art, but that is not a risk that traps the contributors to this volume. Rather than narrowing the terms of discussion, the authors here trace art's own engagement with its presence as art to demonstrate the complexity of the questions these early modern artworks raise. While the editors conceived their project largely in terms of paintings involving the human figure, several essays here are concerned with architectural representations and cityscapes. Indeed, pictorial representation of architecture lies at the heart of some of the most exciting thinking in the book. Christopher Heuer explores the depiction of architectural object as image, the significant presence of the figura or overt facsimile in sixteenth-century northern art. He investigates the depiction and copying outside the Holy Land of its pilgrimage places, such as the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, in terms of figura – a term that encompassed bodily instantiation and prophecy as well as the form of a building, its mental image and its representation. He argues that the strange two-tiered blind niche, the cave of the Nativity in Jerusalem, in a panel painting of Members of the Jerusalem Broederschap of 1520 by an anonymous Amsterdam Master, acts as something beyond sign, outside of history. He argues that as figura, the grotto ‘lays bare’, rather than merely symbolizes, ‘the sacred charge’ of that site (144). That Michelangelo's architecture works to undermine assumed architectural certainties and formal conventions through visual tension, contradiction and uncertainty is generally accepted, but Cammy Brothers develops this notion to claim that it sprang from a position of genuine uncertainty on Michelangelo's part – arguing her point tightly through two sixteenth-century responses to the Medici Chapel and Laurentian Library. Thus, for instance, the conventional predominance of sculpture over architecture is questioned and undermined, not by simple inversion but from within, in order to establish a new basis for knowledge and artistic invention. Interrogating aporia affords new interpretations of the negotiations of difference. Several chapters delineate the ways in which gender and sexuality occupy, produce, or emerge from the crucial dichotomies and discontinuities within pictorial fields or across media; several probe the play between spirit and emphatically material rendering. In a rich and crafty discussion, Lorenzo Pericolo discusses Rembrandt's Danaë (1636) via Panofsky's lapidary interpretation of it. Once again the slipperiness of eroticism and sexuality emerges at the heart of the painting's indeterminacy, including its anticipatory qualities. But in his unveiling of Rembrandt's underscoring of the physiology of amorous anticipation, Pericolo also exposes the limitations of Panofsky's periodizing eye. Panofksy's reading of the painting's curious configurations of its subject in terms of ‘baroque subjectivism’ meant that its innovations became indecipherable as more than a symptom of a universal trend in seventeenth-century art. For Pericolo the painting is more and less than a depiction of Danaë. He argues that in rendering his subject ambiguous Rembrandt deliberately undermined claims to the status of history painting through the conventions of intelligibility and the heroic mode as construed by contemporaneous art theory. Inevitably not all the essays published here participate directly in the questions posed so brilliantly by the editors. Stephen J. Campbell probes the way in which secular painting produced in Venice in the sixteenth century engages in metaphoric combinations, forging poetic connections visually between the human figure and nature, just as the description of nature emerged as an independent genre. He argues that Titian incorporates the metaphoric character of Giorgione's art, such that bodies and their actions become metaphors of sight and touch, and painting is conceived in terms of its sensory dimensions. Tactility and opticality align and oppose each other to not only structure painting but materialize the image. Thus he shows that interest in the physical and material basis of human nature is intimately involved in the vigorous hatching and suturing at work in Renaissance prints. Jeanette Kohl examines Renaissance portrait busts, particularly the so-called Platonic Youth (1440) attributed to Donatello in the Bargello, in terms of the aporia they apparently embody, to argue that their apparent lack, their silences and avoidances, can better be understood, partly in relation to the reliquary bust and through late medieval and early Renaissance body parts, taxonomy and concepts, to artfully propose an aesthetics and ethics of the gaze in the difficult, highly codified rites of passage to homosociability in fifteenth-century Florence. For Patricia Emison, ‘it is as though we confronted Erwin Panofsky's crux of disguised symbolism on the scale of the whole work rather than the discrete motif: to interpret, or not to interpret; to interpret at length, or concisely? Did the demand for novelty spark the talk of god-given artistry, or was it more the other way round?’ (73). Emison argues in an engaging examination of specific artworks including Bramante's puzzling, but evidently ambitious engraving, in which a grandiose and partly ruinous basilica appears to assume the part of protagonist and Dürer's Melencolia of 1514, that their content ‘approaches vestigial status’ (75). While acknowledging that these artworks decline to make ‘clear narrative sense’ for very good reasons, she nevertheless retains the notion that artworks ‘construct meaning’ (83). One cannot help wondering about the possibility that the work that such artworks undertake might be to question the very grounds on which meaning is apparent or possible. The relentless focus on high status canonical artworks could be questioned. It is one thing to argue that canonical artworks anticipate future events; it would be quite another to decipher the ways in which non-canonical works set in motion potentiality that was not taken up. Might the apparent limitations or deformations of some non-canonical artworks also be marks of aporia and interrogation of conventions to which the teleology of the canonical makes us less open? Arguably, too, the authors are sharper on form than on matter, the question of which is sometimes too hastily assumed in both the editors’ introduction and in the essays that follow. But the fundamental questions that are explored so eloquently here are vital for the practice of art history, not only in the early modern period, but way beyond. Colour images would have increased the beauty of the book, but also its price. In any case, Ashgate can afford to be proud of this publication.

title: “Doing Away with Darkness”
abstract: Walking into First Presbyterian Church in downtown Tallahassee, Florida, one is struck by the beauty of the emptiness of the place—the walls are completely bare, the glass unstained, not a crucifix in sight.1 Here is the telos of Reformed iconoclasm. But it isn't only the lack of painted icons, of crucifixes, or of painted glass that's so striking.2 It isn't, in other words, merely the absence of something that one finds to be aesthetically moving at First Pres., Tallahassee. The interior of the church is positively beautiful. It's beautiful despite the lack of any art form or the presence of any color altogether. The gleaming brightness of the whitewashed walls is made brighter by the abundant sunshine that pours in through clear-glass windows, with contrast provided by the black-painted trim on the pews and railing. The grayish-blue, carpeted interiors of the churches of this reviewer's youth did not conjure any such aesthetic response, or really any response whatsoever.3 Theological proclivities aside, Zwingli's 1524 proclamation after the interior walls of the churches in Zurich had been stripped of icons and whitewashed (“The walls are beautifully white!”) becomes understandable here. And it is the response evoked by the sheer whiteness of the Reformed church interior—the fact that it is aesthetically and, perhaps, emotionally affective—that Victoria George is attempting to explain in her book Whitewash and the New Aesthetic of the Protestant Reformation. The purpose of the book is to add a new chapter to the long-standing narrative of sixteenth-century (particularly Reformed)4 iconoclasm, which narrative tends to reduce the movement to just that: iconoclasm—namely, that the Huldrych Zwinglis and John Calvins of the Reformed movement argued only that the adoration of icons in worship is deleterious to Christian piety and that the subsequent whitewashing of walls (a primary mode of covering over painted images) served as a way of simply “painting out,” of image obliteration. George, however, argues that the use of whitewash “is a representation in its own right” (xx), a “painting in” as well as a painting out, and that to understand it only as a cost-effective way of hiding a high-liturgical past is to leave out a significant aspect of the story.Because there is basically no direct evidence that the major thinkers of Reformed iconoclasm imagined whitewash to be a theologically loaded, symbolic expression of various things the color white might be associated with theologically,5 the author employs a sort of kitchen sink approach6 in an attempt to provide sufficient cumulative evidence to convince the reader that there are decent reasons to think that the use of whitewash was a virtually inevitable consequence that followed from the “color-thinking” of Protestant theologians like Zwingli and Calvin, whose respective cities (Zurich and Geneva) carried out the earliest and most thoroughgoing iconoclastic raids. But, as is often the feeling of those on the receiving end of the kitchen sink approach, this reviewer has come away somewhat uncertain about the ultimate success of the venture. The book certainly has its virtues: the primary question itself, that is, whether we might imagine Protestant whitewash as its own form of iconography7—despite its obviousness to anyone acculturated with the common inversion tactics of postmodern critique—is an interesting question, and one that has apparently hardly been asked before, much less received book-length, scholarly attention. There are good and detailed descriptions of the decision-making processes (including documentary evidence of memoranda from various “councils” and “disputations”) revolving around the question of images in the major centers of Reformed Protestantism (especially Switzerland, the Netherlands, and England).8 By the end, the reader has a pretty good hold on the sixteenth-century iconoclastic controversies continent-wide, including all major events and figures. Chapter 3, “An Historical Overview of Whitewashing,” provides a broad and informative history of the process and employment of whitewash in a religious context from the ninth to the twenty-first century. To this end, the book is also replete with some seventy glossy images of white-interiored churches, Renaissance paintings that employ white in a theologically significant manner, etchings, engravings, and a Saab campaign.9 One even learns the ins and outs of the chemical process of making and using whitewash. (And who knew there was a journal called Concrete Quarterly!?)Probably the most important contribution, and really the heart of the matter for George, is the treatment (in the final two chapters) of Zwingli's and Calvin's theologies as they relate to color. No doubt they represent the first attempts to tease out the “color-thinking” of these two sixteenth-century giants. Fundamental to these chapters is the contention that Zwingli's and Calvin's radical transcendentalism, combined with their appreciation of the color white as symbolically representative of (for example) divine light, on the one hand, and proto-Puritan this-worldly asceticism, on the other, is directly linked to the Reformed tendency to whitewash the interior walls of their churches. Whiteness, the argument goes, is the closest approximation of a representation of God's inscrutable nature in material form. “In the context of religious faith and the worship of God,” George writes, “the whitewashed wall represents two things anagogically: first, the immaterial state of God's being in virtue of its being ‘not-colour’ and, therefore not of the corporeal world. Simultaneously, in virtue of its imagelessness, it represents the transcendence of God's being” (403–4). Color is deceptive; it's a cloak. But white (a noncolor, for the author's purposes) is honest and true. The argument rests on the author's further (perhaps more problematical) contention that there is an “intuitive connection between the concepts of immateriality, transcendence and spirituality, and the colour white in the context of representation” (404). If one is willing to grant this “intuitive connection” then the argument running through these two chapters makes a certain amount of sense;10 namely, there is a theological and not merely economic basis for painting church interiors white. However, the “radical transcendentalist” reading of Calvin's theology, which is a sine qua non of the book's central argument, lacks a certain kind of nuance that recent Calvin scholarship has sought to provide.11 The author's insistence that the slogan finitum non est capax infiniti12 is the key to understanding Calvin's thought places her firmly on a Barthian trajectory in terms of Calvin's twentieth-century interpreters. And while I'm not given, as are many Calvin scholars and Calvinist theologians of recent decades, to denounce altogether Barth's reading of Calvin,13 there have been several important advancements in Calvin studies that complicate it, many of which bear on the question of images and the role of sight in Calvin's thought. To be reckoned with in particular, but nowhere mentioned in George's book, is Randall Zachman's 2007 Image and Word in the Theology of John Calvin (Notre Dame Press), which mounts a sustained critique of Barth's reading of Calvin and argues that a weak form of natural theology might be salvaged in Calvin's thought.14 Zachman's distinction between “living” and “dead” images in Calvin's theology, the former of which—being created by God, or which are manifest as God's works in the world—do have significance for the Christian's knowledge of God (especially after the Christian has put on the “spectacles of scripture”), while the latter (human-made icons, etc.) do not, would seem to pose problems for George's repeated insistence that nothing material or visual or in color15 can contribute to meaningful theological knowledge.16The book has other problems. Take the minor first: it could have benefited, especially, from a heavier editorial hand. Structural and typographical problems force the reader to do some unnecessary heavy lifting.17 In general these might be a mere nuisance, but occasionally organizational issues affect the coherence of parts of the book and the ability to discern and follow the arguments therein. Chapter 2, “A Short Trip Through Colour Theory,” for example, is a bit disorienting: the reader is led through 2,500 years of color theory, but not necessarily in chronological order. Alberti, Plato, Aristotle, Aquinas, Newton, Wittgenstein, Plotinus, the early Church Fathers, the Oxford English Dictionary, Cicero, and finally the Bible are all on offer here. Objections to the kitchen sink approach aside, the author is never quite clear on why modern thinkers like Newton and Wittgenstein matter, or why it's helpful to invoke them in a study primarily on the sixteenth century.18 The Bible eventually also gets a chapter all to itself, where much material is repeated, but not until three chapters later.19 Equally frustrating, and arguably more problematic, is the way the author uses/does not use primary languages. In the chapter on color in the Bible, for example, sometimes the original Greek of the New Testament is given, sometimes it isn't.20 The original Hebrew is never provided in discussions of Old Testament passages.21 Confusingly, when the King James Version is quoted the author always also provides the Vulgate original alongside, as if the KJV were a translation from the Latin. (It isn't.22) Moreover, the KJV is a seventeenth-century translation, and the Vulgate was rejected by Protestant humanists like Zwingli and Calvin as a useful Latin version in the wake of corrections provided by, especially, Jacques Lefevre d'Etaples and Erasmus.23 Why do either figure in?24German isn't provided in the chapter on Zwingli's thought, nor is there any Latin given in the chapter on Calvin's. This is problematic not on account of this reviewer's admitted penchant for the Romantic, but because many of the author's arguments are language oriented; to wit: “The suppression of colour in order to transcend the material is evident in Zwingli's thought. Where the Good is ‘painted’ [Zwingli says], it is painted ‘with clear strokes.’ Purity, which is the absence of admixture (pollution), is ‘untaintedness’, a colour term in origin” (332). The author uses such examples (which are in fact few) to argue that Zwingli's interest in color is linked to his interest in purity. But what is the word Zwingli is using here for clear? It's not obvious that he's talking about color at all, at least in English. “Clear” might mean “colorless” or “transparent,” but it might also very well mean “evident” or “obvious,” or even “adept” if referring specifically to the painter's strokes. And what is the word Zwingli is using for untaintedness? Is it a “colour term in origin” in Zwingli's Swiss German? Or in English? What is the author referring to here? We, the readers, have no idea. But, given the insistence on the part of the author that Zwingli doesn't very often use color language at all, and given the author's stated recognition that extrapolation is therefore a tenuous venture, it would seem to be paramount that in those few cases where he possibly uses “color” language we have a very clear idea what he means; and this would involve, to this reviewer's mind at least, some mention of the original language.25Trivia aside, the author has a tendency to hedge when dealing with the crucial arguments of the book, which can be disconcerting. She oscillates between admissions of speculation regarding the reasons for whitewashing walls in Zurich and Geneva and much stronger claims that Zwingli's and Calvin's theologies demand the outcome of whitewash, writing at one point that the theologies of both thinkers “essentially mandate the use of this color” (412). She wants to insist, simultaneously, on the novelty of Protestant attitudes toward the symbolism of the color white, and its well-entrenched nature in the history of Western thought. She writes, “The aesthetic values introduced by the Reformers radicalized the architectural interiors of the ecclesiastical world” (332). But basically the entire book up to this point has been an attempt to demonstrate that the Reformers' aesthetic values weren't novel at all: Plato, Aristotle, Plotinus, Pseudo-Dionysius, Thomas Aquinas—all these fellows held the same position regarding the equivalence of white with (divine) light and black with darkness (= evil). Indeed, the connection between white and purity is occasionally described as an “a priori fact.” I can imagine an argument that suggests that Zwingli and Calvin more fully appreciate the symbolic values of whiteness or that they invest in its significance through practical application, but no such argument is given; nor is the evidence of their associations of whiteness with relatively significant theological import overwhelming enough for the reader to comfortably infer something along these lines (indeed, the author readily acknowledges that the evidence isn't quite there).More convincing is the argument, which appears in various forms, that Neoplatonist26 understandings of beauty in immateriality drive Zwingli's and Calvin's sentiments against pollution, admixture, and so on and might thus be thought to undergird their appreciation of whitewashed walls.27 But strength is relative here, and there is, admittedly, some difficulty in discerning precisely what it is the author wants to accomplish with these arguments vis-à-vis the “color question” and the use of whitewash. In the introduction, the author claims two purposes for the book, each of which brings along its own methodological baggage. The first (call it quasi-Weberian), wants ideas to do some work in terms of social/historical change: Zwingli's and Calvin's theologies demand that the walls be whitewashed (as opposed, say, to being painted blue), and the inexorable logic of their theology has resulted, in some sense, in the perpetuation of white interiors in Reformed churches.28 The second (call it quasi-Marxist) wants material culture to do a similar sort of work, such that “whitewashing becomes as much a proselytising agent of change as it is a form of discipline and a critical element of emerging identity” (7). The first turns out to be quite prevalent, especially in the later chapters (on Zwingli's and Calvin's thought), but the second is never really dealt with at all after the introduction, and one wonders whether it appears only as a kind of obligatory nod to reigning academic tendencies. A second-order form of wavering, but one that reveals itself as central, arises from the author's tentativeness regarding the central question of the book: whether whitewashing walls can be necessarily linked to theological sensibilities, or whether it was simply cost-effective.29And, again, the general paucity of evidence regarding when and why churches were whitewashed, especially in the sixteenth century, makes this tentativeness stand out. The move from aniconism as an ideal to whitewash as a necessarily linked positive aesthetic value, it would seem, needs a bit more historical work done before we refer to “the aesthetic values introduced by the Reformers” as that which legitimates the removal or obliteration of images in sixteenth-century churches. We might wonder, then, given the long-standing symbolic importance of the color white, why such forms of iconoclasm didn't occur sooner.30 And because the author keeps mentioning (to her credit) that whitewash was, after all, the cheapest way of repainting a wall, perhaps it's better to point to the ongoing radical appeals to destroy things “made by human hands” when trying to account for iconoclastic tendencies.31 I don't deny the validity of the book's weaker argument, namely, that the choice of whitewash (as opposed to some other color) didn't come free of aesthetic, or even aesthetico-religious, consideration. But I find unconvincing the stronger argument, that a preliminary identification of whiteness and holiness accounts for the subsequent destruction of images used in worship—that is, that whitewash and iconoclasm are inextricably and necessarily linked (by dint of some kind of unexplained intellectual-symbolic-aesthetic logical coercion) in terms of an overarching theological motivation.Arriving at the conclusion, it's frustrating to find the author asking the same questions that were posed in the beginning, and with seemingly no confidence that they've been answered over four hundred pages later: “Was the coat of whitewash purely a practical matter, or was it a political act? An act of violent, purposeful destruction directed at the Papacy, or an opportunistic form of graffiti committed by an enthusiastic sector of the public? Was it incidental to the elimination of representation within the church along with other ‘externals’, or did it signify theological meaning according to a generalized sense of impetus to reform?” (424). The author doesn't seem to know the answers to these questions, and neither does the reader. The book then concludes with the following (note: inconclusive) sentence: “A primary goal of this study was to discover whether a theological basis for whitewashing existed, and whether a particular way of thinking about the colour white might be discerned which could be said to have motivated certain precedent-setting reformers to arrive at this particular solution or even to have demanded it of them” (429). It certainly could be said that there exists a theological basis for whitewashing, and it could be said that this theological basis motivated reformers in their whitewashing, but given the author's own palpable insecurities about whether it's been shown to be the case, we don't know whether we shouldsay it or not. The symbolic identification of the color white with intellectual enlightenment, made metaphorically at the beginning of Calvin's Institutes, is invoked by the author for its import in the context of whitewash. Given the subject matter of the book, it's difficult to ignore a certain irony attending Wittgenstein's question, placed as an epigram to the second chapter and as an epitaph here: “Isn't white that which does away with darkness?”

title: Nobody Can Harm You, Nobody Can Charm You: Efik Nnabo Society Masquerades of Calabar, Nigeria
abstract: all photos by Onyile Bassey Onyile except where otherwise notedThe Nnabo society is an institution of the Efik people of Calabar, Cross River State, Nigeria. Formerly charged with martial duties, Nnabo masquerades today serve various functions—including spiritual protection and public performances to honor deceased members and the Efik Obong, or paramount ruler—while offering a visually rich display of heritage that speaks to a larger complex of masquerade societies previously found throughout the Cross River basin. Here, we address the lacuna in published sources about Nnabo by introducing the primary masquerade characters and their roles based on interviews with society members in Calabar.Nowadays Nnabo highlights the warriorlike prowess displayed by energetic young men in their attempts to intimidate and frighten onlookers during public performances. That the masquerades seek to inspire fear is no surprise, considering their former roles among the Efik, which included warfare (Figs. 1, 5, 7). Hence, Nnabo connotes the fearlessness and steady vigilance required to protect the dignity and integrity of the Efik people. While a few members in Calabar today might still desire to regain its former power, Nnabo long ago ceded its martial function to government and now performs primarily to honor fellow members during events such as commemorative funerals, or the installation of a new Obong. Nnabo also provides public entertainment at the holidays (e.g., the annual Christmas carnival of masquerades in Calabar), and may perform during private functions.We were repeatedly told that, prior to the colonial period, Nnabo led the way onto the battlefield during times of confrontation or war. Its masquerades were charged with intimidating the enemy and removing any malignant spiritual forces they may have incurred. In times of peace, certain members—the Nsibidi Nnabo—carried out the executions of condemned persons ordered by the Obong. The Efik phrase nedseo nsibidi refers to the act of execution.The origin of Nnabo is shrouded in history, although Efik oral history traces it to the region of the Ejagham peoples of the upper Cross River region. According to members of the Owanese group, Nnabo is not an Efik term, but rather is Qua/Ejagham, because they “owned” the word.1 However, the precise meaning was not proffered because it's “nsibidi”—that is, a secret. Apart from its general connotation as a “war dance,” members noted that Nnabo also means, “Everybody knows that something happens” or, more succinctly, “Action!” It may be that the group originated with, or was inspired by, a Qua/Ejaham or Efut source, as was the men's Leopard Society, known as Ekpe amongst the Efik of Calabar (Latham 1973:36; Leib and Romano 1984:48).The institution of Nnabo is not limited to the Calabar region. A Nnabo masquerade costume seen by the authors at the Oron Museum in 2004 indicates the group is widespread throughout the southern Cross River region. Its label read:According to the Ibibio scholar A.E. Udoh, the Ibibio of Akwa Ibom State also had a related group called “Nsibidi,” which, like Ekpe, “had secret signs known only to members” (1983:54).2 However, unlike the well-known Ekpe society, which is organized by grade and whose members are initiated by invitation, membership in Nnabo is open to any interested person, male or female—but men perform all of the masquerades.The characters of Nnabo masquerades act aggressively because they were meant to strike terror into the hearts and minds of enemies met on the battlefield, criminals condemned to death under Nnabo's sword, or those who would threaten the Obong, whom Nnabo is charged to protect. While these sentiments still hold true today, the powerful aura and imposing appearance of Nnabo masquerades mostly serve to intimidate on-lookers rather than martial foes (Fig. 1). Mostly. Because it surprised no one when, in the years immediately following the Nigerian civil war (1967–1970), the public performances of Nnabo grew so unruly amongst rival associations that they were occasionally banned by the government. As recently as 2003, the Cross River state police forbade Nnabo from performing at the annual Christmas carnival, Calabar's largest masquerade venue (Onah 2003:n.p.). This event has become a massive draw for domestic tourists and therefore is potentially a lucrative event for the Nnabo members who perform. Hence, they decided to keep things more civil from then on.We were fortunate to be invited into the home of Atafiong Okon Ata (a.k.a. Ikwa Afang) in Calabar South municipality. He is a former Nnabo president of the (Owanese) Nka Okutama Isong Efik Eburutu group, one of the seven Nnabo associations of Calabar.3 Also present were fellow Nnabo members Dr. E.E. Ironbar (clan head); Mr. Aniekan (Financial Secretary); Louis Edem Duke (Secretary General); Bassey Offiong Okon (Youth Leader); and Efeffiong Otu Effiong—a.k.a. Efere Otong, “Okra Soup” (Protocol Officer). Their combined presence, no doubt, was meant to validate the information provided to us. Atafiong opened the meeting in modern fashion, by reciting a Christian prayer—after which his fellows replied, “Amen”—then poured libation onto the earth to honor the ancestors. He wore the distinctive indigo-dyed cotton wrapper (ukara) covered with nsibidi signs,4 a cloth that is the sole prerogative of Ekpe society members. Atafiong later emphasized that Nnabo is distinct from Ekpe, although they both use nsibidi as a secret code to transmit information to members. Nonetheless, Ekpe is the most prestigious Efik men's society, which explains why Ata proclaimed his membership in it as well.According to Efik oral history, Abasi, or Almighty God, provided Nnabo troupe members with the knowledge to create antidotes—recipes for specific ibok (medicines) using combinations of plants—so that humankind could protect itself during war or conflict with neighboring villages. Nnabo personifies the most potent of ibok used for protection against impending danger. It is one of many masquerades in Efik culture that are believed to be imbued with spiritual prowess and clairvoyance. A Nnabo masker properly empowered with ibok is considered to be able to perceive hidden danger in order to overcome it.Before any Nnabo performance, many rituals must be conducted, including the singing of sacred songs to empower the medicines that protect Nnabo performers. The rites also include setting the “table,” or altar, called okpokoro Nnabo (Fig. 2), which is placed on the floor with members seated around it. The okpokoro contains a plantain leaf with two old swords crossed over it; nkoi-ebion (porcupine quill); a portion of iduot (a reddish powder obtained by scraping the bark of the ukpa tree, Pterocarpus soyauxii, which is used as a medicinal ointment); and charcoal (ukan or nkan), a metaphor of the past. Here nkan and iduot act as antidotes to any malevolent charm present on or around the altar. Also included is a bottle of locally brewed gin wrapped with a red scarf, an egg, and a string of seven cowry shells. In Efik folklore, itiaba (seven) is a sacred number having special powers. It signifies completeness, the perfection of a complete cycle. The symbolism invested in the number seven in Efik folklore can be linked to the origin of creation (and for this reason, Nnabo maskers generally perform in groups of seven).As the gathering is called to order, libation is poured onto the earth to invite the spirits of departed members and the ancestors of the larger Efik community to join the gathering. At the same time, the spirit of Nnabo and all of its powerful medicines are invoked. Immediately after the pouring of libation, the egg on the okpokoro is picked up protectively by its custodian. The egg symbolizes life and motherhood. Essentially, it represents Ndem Efik, a tutelary deity of the Efik people associated with the rivers and seas who is revered by Nnabo. Eggs are central components in Ndem rituals because of their potent medicinal and healing properties. Cowry shells, which come from the sea, also pay homage to Ndem. They solicit protection from evildoers. Cowries were also a precolonial form of currency and so are symbolic of wealth and status (Eyo 1979:42–44, 58). The plantain leaf represents nature and provides the assurance of unity among Nnabo members. The crossed swords literally project a show of strength. But their four ends also symbolize the cardinal points of the earth and the coming together of the spiritual and human realms. The red scarf represents blood shed in war.5Nnabo troupes consist of several types of performers, each with specific roles that contribute to the total harmony of the Nnabo performance. Chief Effiong Effiom noted that there are many different characters represented by Nnabo masquerades, including Edua Nnabo (Nnabo dog) or Edua Ino (dog thief); Nsibidi Nnabo; Idem Nnabo; Mkpokoro (human skull); Ayabom Nnabo (male Nnabo); Eka Nnabo (Nnabo mother); and Anansa.6 This section describes them according to their seven hierarchal orders, which corresponds to how the troupe advanced on their enemies during wartime. All the Nnabo masquerades wear strands of nyok (seed shells from the ebo tree), which jingle rhythmically as they perform.Before any performance or outing, Nnabo troupe members employ a medicine (ndomo) to predict the outcome of their impending activity. Ndomo is made up of short strands of broom, tied with a piece of red cloth, and an egg. Effiong told us that, as part of the consultation rites, the egg is smashed on the floor beside the broom, and depending on layout of the empty eggshell, the future of the impending performance may be predicted. If interior of the broken eggshells lie facing the floor, this would indicate that a problem is imminent. On the other hand, if the insides of the shells are visible, this would signal a positive outcome.7Leading the way is Edua Nnabo, the scout, who keeps ahead of the other performers as they move through town. It vigilantly seeks out enemy ibok, and is heavily armed with its own ibok to ward away their effects (Fig. 3). This character also acts as the custodian of gifts given to the troupe in appreciation of their performance, in order to inspect them for any hidden ibok before they are handed out to members of the troupe. Edua Nnabo's costume bears some resemblance to that of Mkpokoro, but is only about half its size. And while Mkpokoro is always in black, Edua Nnabo's garments may vary in color, though red is preferred. In both hands, Edua Nnabo holds stems of the cocoyam (Colocasia esculenta), which are used to scare off anyone who might get in its way (in fact, the fluid from this plant can be very irritating on contact with human skin). The face cover of this Nnabo is very much like that of Mkpokoro, though its headgear is different and varies depending on the choices of its maker.Closely following Edua Nnabo is Nsibidi Nnabo, the security force of the entourage, whose appearance informs the public of an impending performance. Nsibidi maskers appear with faces and bodies painted with charcoal and heads adorned with mkpatari (Seleginelia canaliculata). Around their waists hang short shirts made from the fiber of young palm frond shoots, ekpin (Elaeis guineensis). Each Nsibidi member also holds a piece of ekpin between their lips to prevent them from speaking during the performance.There are three characters represented by Nsibidi Nnabo. The executioners bear a machete with the right hand, and with the left, a basket—claimed to be full of water. Of course, the claim that a loosely woven basket could contain water is preposterous. The boast is meant to demonstrate the power of Nnabo charms to achieve the impossible … and also to intimidate an opponent. Another type of Nsibidi Nnabo again wields a machete with the right hand, and with the left hand holds okpoho, a long wooden hook cut from a Y-shaped branch, which formerly was used to secure the heads of those sentenced to execution. Following closely is the “medicine man,” or charm-bearer, who carries a rectangular box filled with skulls symbolizing the victims of previous wars—a warning to potential enemies. He is the heart of the Nnabo performance and is fiercely protected (Fig. 4).Altogether, the Nsibidi troupe is usually made up of about twenty people. In their midst is a man in plain clothes, who blows the obukpon (antelope horn) to announce the presence of Nnabo. He remains in close proximity to the charm-bearer throughout the performance. The horn blower is dressed in white from head to toe, which echoes the appearance of Ndem Efik. The sound of the obukpon alerts everyone of the approaching Nnabo entourage.8Together with Nsibidi Nnabo and the charm bearer, the drummers dictate the dancing steps of Nnabo. Following the drummers is the character called Mkpokoro (skull), an unpredictable and potentially violent image (Figs. 1, 5). This figure wears an oversized black gown trimmed on both arms with tightly woven brown raffia (Raphia farinifera or R. ruffia). Its startling appearance is enhanced by the display of actual human skulls that stare ahead menacingly. The relics, members claim, are those of slain enemies—the spoils of war. Bold, cryptic symbols (nsibidi) cover the masquerade's “face.” Mkpokoro is the scavenger who picks things from the ground as it moves along, covering them with its gown. It is believed that anything Mkpokoro covers in this way will disappear, hence onlookers carefully avoid its approach. According to Efik tradition, it was the duty of Nnabo to protect the integrity of the Obong—and by extension that of the Efik people as well—in part by overt visual intimidation. Mkpokoro's costume, in other words, represents a legacy of studiously developed psychological warfare.Appearing with Mkpokoro are the Idem Nnabo, which represent the “spirit” of Nnabo (Fig. 6). They sing and speak with a disguised voice. They are the dance specialists of the troupe, and are recognized as the best entertainers. The costume of Idem Nnabo is similar to that of Edua Nnabo and Mkpokoro. They hold a broom (ayan) in their right hand, which they wave around to ward off the effects of any charms that might be lingering about, and with their left hand hold okpoho. Like Mkpokoro, these Nnabo masquerades are adorned with skulls as part of their headgear. However, the major difference is that these Nnabo wear woven multicolored knitted fiber suits (esik), similar to the Ekpe costume. On their backs are vibrantly colored layers of raffia. The top of the costume is also raffia, thickly layered, including a section dyed with indigo. One layer covers most of the head and features a small skull dangling over the forehead; the second drapes over the shoulder. Beneath the skull is a red cloth masking the bearer's face. The costume displays large-scale nsibidi signs (e.g. arcs, circles, and cruciforms) boldly delineated in cowry shells, the archaic currency. We were told these nsibidi motifs constituted the “face” of the masquerade. Cowries, as noted previously, are also symbolic of Ndem. They serve as powerful transformative medicines that, according to Ata, “imbue the masquerade with fear … once on a masquerade it turns to another thing. It can harm.” Moreover, in Nnabo ontology, cowries are considered the “teeth” of Nnabo.But for the masquerader himself, cowries have an opposite, protective effect, which was explained poetically by Ata during our 2009 meeting: “Nobody can harm you, nobody can charm you.”The most feared and potentially violent character in the entire Nnabo troupe is called Ayabom. Due to the rituals involved in its preparation, as well as the presumed effects the costume has upon its wearer, Ayabom rarely appears in public. When it does, it never appears unescorted and is restrained by a leash tied around the waist, which broadcasts even more loudly the simmering potential for chaos implied by its grisly countenance (Fig. 7). This image represents a kind of visual assault that, in times past, was meant to psychologically terrorize its enemies with shock and awe. Despite the reality that the colonial government long ago ended the martial role of Nnabo, its form is maintained by the society as a part of their history. We think it is likely that the actual skulls and bones used to create the masquerades illustrated here were recovered during the construction of the University of Calabar in the 1970s, when the cemetery located there was destroyed.The most prominent member of the Nnabo masquerade lineup is Eka Nnabo, the leader of the troupe who embodies calmness and sanity, life and rebirth (Fig. 3). She represents Anansa, the goddess of the sea. She “cools” Nnabo maskers with her graceful dancing. According to our informant, the group's protocol officer, Efeffiong Otu Effiong, Eka Nnabo personifies the mother of humanity, despite the fact that the performer is a man. Her costume is radically different from the other Nnabo. She wears a carved face mask, adorned with multicolored feathers and an elaborate hairdo. She holds a walking stick in each hand and wears a multicolored akasi around her waist.
